comparison.summary: Five JavaScript approaches are available here. The first uses a shorter exact-ID implementation with comma-separated pair keys and a binary search that returns lo when its bounds meet. It takes expected O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space with bounded-size keys. The rolling-hash and three suffix approaches remain available.
details: The exact-ID version builds power-of-two block levels with flat Maps keyed by `${left},${right}` and assigns each new pair the ID map.size. Each tested window is identified by its first and last block IDs, whose blocks cover the whole sequence. It takes expected O(n log n) time with expected constant-time Map operations and O(n log n) space, treating keys as bounded in size; n is the number of elements. Keys have at most 13 characters under the problem constraints, though creating and hashing those strings still adds overhead.

The rolling-hash version binary-searches the length and groups windows by hash, then compares their actual elements before combining occurrence counts. It takes O(n log n + C) time with expected constant-time Map operations, where C counts all exact element comparisons, and O(n) space. A conservative worst-case time bound is O(n³ log n).
The simple suffix version copies and sorts whole suffixes, then compares neighboring suffixes directly. It is exact, but takes O(n² log n) time with O(n log n) sort comparisons and O(n²) space.

The optimized suffix array version uses rank doubling and stable counting sort, then Kasai’s algorithm for adjacent LCP values. It applies the same unique-prefix formula in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The suffix automaton propagates occurrence counts through the shorterId tree and finds the shortest length represented by a node that occurs once. It takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

The older Python solution binary-searches the length and counts rolling hashes without checking the actual elements, taking O(n log n) time and O(n) space. That hash-only comparison is incorrect for nums = [1,20,2,1,20,2]: it returns 3 instead of 2. With base 19, [1,20] and [2,1] both hash to 39, hiding the unique pair [2,1]. All five saved JavaScript solutions return the correct answer 2.

Choosing a base larger than the values prevents that base-19 example from colliding, but modular collisions can still happen. The saved rolling-hash version keeps separate exact-window groups under the same hash; the first solution instead uses exact sequence IDs throughout.

solutions.title: Binary search + exact sequence IDs
solutions.approach: Build exact IDs for blocks whose lengths are powers of two. Single-value blocks use their values as IDs. At each later level, form the comma-separated key `${left},${right}` from the two half IDs; a new key receives map.size as its ID, and an existing key reuses its ID. Then binary-search the smallest valid window length. For each candidate k, choose the largest power-of-two block that fits using Math.floor(Math.log2(k)). Identify each window by its first and last block IDs and count the comma-separated keys. These two blocks cover the whole window, so matching keys mean equal sequences. If a key appears once, keep mid as the upper bound; otherwise move the lower bound to mid + 1. Return lo when the bounds meet.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) expected, treating short keys as bounded in size and assuming expected constant-time Map operations
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log n) for bounded-size keys
notes: The comma-separated string preserves both integer IDs and their order. IDs are local to one block level; 0 is valid, so use map.has(key) to check whether a pair already has an ID.
The first and last blocks cover the whole window and may overlap. When k is a power of two, both IDs describe the same block, and the window is still counted once.
Keys have at most 13 characters under the problem constraints. Creating and hashing strings adds overhead, while their bounded size gives the stated expected O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space.
solutions.intuition: Instead of comparing every element whenever two windows might match, give equal sequences the same exact ID. A long block can be identified by the IDs of its two halves. For any window length, two overlapping blocks of a power-of-two length cover the whole window, so their pair of IDs identifies that window exactly. This makes checking one length fast enough to binary-search the shortest unique one.
hints: If a sequence occurs once, extending that occurrence by one element at either valid end keeps it unique. What does that imply about the lengths worth testing?
Assign IDs to blocks of lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on. Two blocks at the same level are equal exactly when their left-half IDs and right-half IDs match.
For a candidate length k, let len be the largest power of two at most k. Pair the block starting at i with the block starting at i + k - len, then count those pairs across all windows.

pseudocode.concept: Find the first window length with an exact sequence ID that appears once.
steps: Use each input value as the ID of its length-1 block.
For each doubled block length, pair the two half IDs and assign one new ID to each distinct pair at that level.
Start the search with lengths 1 through the full array length.
For the middle length, choose the largest power-of-two block that fits.
Count each window by the pair of IDs for its first and last blocks, after visiting every window of that length.
If a pair occurs once, keep the middle length as the upper bound; otherwise move the lower bound past it.
Return the remaining length when the bounds meet.

solutions.explanation:
1. The first level contains the input values, so equal length-1 blocks already have equal IDs. At every later level, a fresh Map assigns the same ID to the same ordered pair of half IDs. By induction, equal IDs at one level mean equal blocks of that level’s length. IDs from different levels are never compared.

2. For a candidate length k, the selected block length len satisfies len <= k < 2 × len. The first block starts at i; the last starts at i + k - len. Both stay inside the window and together cover every element. They may overlap or coincide, which is safe: equality of both blocks is equivalent to equality of the complete windows.

3. The comma separates the two integer IDs in each key, so different ordered pairs remain distinct. Count all windows before looking for a count of 1; a window that looks unique early may appear again later. Overlapping occurrences still count as separate occurrences.

4. The search condition is monotone. Any unique window shorter than the array can be extended at one valid end. A duplicate of that extension would also duplicate the original window at the same offset, which is impossible. Therefore, once a length works, every larger length works too.

5. When the middle length works, setting hi to mid keeps that valid candidate. Otherwise, setting lo to mid + 1 discards only lengths that cannot work. The full array is always unique because it has only one starting position, so the final common bound is the smallest valid length.

solutions.title: Binary search + rolling hash
solutions.approach: Binary-search the smallest length for which some continuous subarray occurs exactly once. For each tested length, build the first window’s polynomial hash, then slide by removing the outgoing value’s weighted contribution, shifting the remaining weights, and adding the incoming value. Store a list of representative windows and occurrence counts under each hash. When hashes match, compare the actual elements before increasing a count; different sequences keep separate groups. After recording every window, a group with count 1 means this length works, so search shorter lengths. Otherwise, search longer lengths. A unique window can always be extended while remaining unique, which makes binary search valid.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n + C) with expected constant-time Map operations; O(n³ log n) conservative worst case

variables.C: Total element comparisons in sameWindow across all tested lengths, including comparisons between matching duplicate windows and between different windows that share a hash.

notes: Equal hashes are only a reason to compare two windows, not proof that they are equal. Exact element checks keep this version correct even when different windows share a hash.
Large inputs with many repeated windows can make exact comparisons expensive. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below offer stronger performance bounds.
solutions.intuition: A rolling hash lets you update a window’s fingerprint by removing its first value and adding its next value. The fingerprint helps find possible matches, but only an element-by-element comparison proves two windows are equal. Once you can count exact occurrences for one length, binary search finds the first length containing a unique window.
hints: A unique window stays unique when extended at a valid end, so the answer can be found by searching over lengths.
Build the first window’s polynomial hash, then reuse it: subtract the outgoing value’s weight, multiply by the base, and add the incoming value.
Equal hashes do not guarantee equal sequences. Keep separate groups within a hash bucket and compare actual window elements before increasing a group’s count.

pseudocode.concept: Use rolling hashes to locate possible matches, verify them exactly, and binary-search the first valid length.
steps: Find the largest input value and choose the base as that value plus one.
Start the search over lengths 1 through the array length, with the full length as a valid answer.
For each tested length, compute the outgoing value’s highest power and build the first window’s hash.
Record a window by finding an equal representative in its hash bucket; increment that group or create a separate group.
Slide through every remaining window by removing, shifting, and adding, recording each window the same way.
After all windows are counted, check whether any exact-sequence group has count 1.
Save successful lengths and search smaller ones; otherwise search larger ones. Return the smallest saved length.

solutions.explanation:
1. The hash treats a window like a base-BASE number, reduced modulo MOD. highestPower is BASE raised to length - 1 modulo MOD, which is the weight of the outgoing element. The first window is built from left to right with repeated multiply-and-add operations.

2. Sliding first subtracts the outgoing element’s weighted contribution. Adding MOD before taking the remainder avoids a negative remainder here. Multiplying by BASE shifts the remaining weights, and adding the incoming element finishes the next window’s hash.

3. Each hash maps to a list of representative windows. sameWindow compares every corresponding element until it finds a difference or reaches the end. Equal sequences share one count; different sequences remain separate even when their hashes collide. These comparisons preserve correctness but can make the implementation slower on repeated or colliding windows.

4. A count of 1 is meaningful only after recording every window of the tested length. The search then uses monotonicity: extending a unique window at a valid end cannot create a duplicate without also duplicating the original window.

5. On success, save mid and continue below it with hi = mid - 1. On failure, move lo to mid + 1. The full array supplies an initial valid answer, so the saved answer is the shortest length that succeeds when the search ends.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: Separate the rolling-hash bookkeeping from C, the actual element comparisons used to verify matches.

phases.label: Build powers and the first hash, slide all windows, and scan groups across O(log n) length checks

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: Map access is expected constant time. Even equal duplicate windows require exact comparisons, so C cannot be dropped. In a conservative worst case, one of O(n) windows may compare against O(n) representatives for O(n) elements each in every length check, giving O(n³ log n) total time. Buckets and representatives for one tested length use O(n) space.

solutions.title: Simple suffix sorting + LCP
solutions.approach: Copy every suffix and sort those arrays lexicographically. For each suffix, compare its elements with the previous and next suffix to find their longest common prefixes (LCP). A unique prefix needs max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 elements; take the smallest such length that fits inside its suffix.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n² log n) with O(n log n) sort comparisons
notes: This version makes the steps easier to follow, but copies n(n + 1) / 2 elements. Use an optimized version for large inputs such as 100,000 numbers.
solutions.intuition: Every subarray is a prefix of the suffix that starts at the same position. After sorting suffixes, the strongest competitors for a suffix’s prefix are its immediate neighbors. To make that prefix unique, it must be longer than the common prefix with both neighbors. The shorter of the two common-prefix lengths is not enough: the other neighbor could still match.
hints: Think of every possible subarray as the beginning of one suffix. Sorting the suffixes puts those with matching prefixes next to each other.
For one suffix, compare its common-prefix length with the previous suffix and with the next suffix. The prefix must outlast both matches.
Try max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1. Ignore this candidate if the suffix does not contain that many elements, then minimize the remaining candidates.

pseudocode.concept: Sort whole suffixes and extend each prefix just beyond its longest neighboring match.
steps: Copy the suffix beginning at every input index.
Sort these arrays lexicographically, with a shorter equal-prefix suffix before a longer one.
For each sorted suffix, count matching initial elements with the previous neighbor and the next neighbor; a missing neighbor contributes zero.
Add one to the larger of those two common-prefix lengths.
If that length fits in the current suffix, use it to lower the best answer.
Return the smallest valid candidate.

solutions.explanation:
1. Copying every suffix exposes every possible starting position. A prefix of one of these suffixes corresponds exactly to a continuous subarray of the original array, so finding the shortest unique prefix covers every possible answer.

2. The comparator checks corresponding values until they differ. If one suffix ends first while all compared values match, that shorter suffix comes first. This is lexicographic order, which keeps all suffixes sharing any chosen prefix in one contiguous group.

3. That contiguous-group property is why two neighbors are sufficient. If any other suffix shares a prefix with the current suffix, an immediate neighbor on that side shares at least that prefix too. Thus the longest common prefix with any competing suffix is the maximum of the two neighboring LCP values.

4. A prefix of length max(prevLcp, nextLcp) still repeats, but one additional element separates it from every competitor. If that extra element does not exist in the suffix, this starting position supplies no unique prefix.

5. Take the minimum candidate over all starting positions. The full input always occurs once as a length-n subarray, so initializing best to n provides a valid answer even before any improvement.

solutions.approach: Sort suffix starting indices without copying the suffixes: rank doubling compares increasingly long prefixes using stable counting sorts. Kasai’s algorithm calculates neighboring LCP values while reusing matches from the previous suffix. For each suffix, compute max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 and take the smallest length that fits inside that suffix.
notes: This optimized version uses the separate function name smallestUniqueSubarraySuffixArray.
solutions.intuition: The suffix-and-LCP idea does not require copying every suffix or repeatedly comparing long arrays. Store suffix starting indices, rank short prefixes, and combine two ranks to sort twice as many elements at a time. Then reuse known matching prefixes while calculating LCP values. The final unique-prefix rule is still one more than the larger neighboring LCP.

steps: Return 1 immediately for a one-element input; otherwise assign ordered ranks to the distinct input values.
Create one suffix starting index for each input position.
For each doubled prefix length, stably counting-sort suffix indices by the second-half rank and then the first-half rank.
Assign new ranks to distinct pairs; stop early when every suffix has a different rank.
Build the inverse suffix-array positions, then scan original starting indices to compute each suffix’s LCP with its sorted predecessor, reusing all but one previous match.
For every suffix, calculate one more than the maximum LCP with its two sorted neighbors.

solutions.explanation:
1. Initial value compression gives equal numbers equal ranks while preserving their order. sa stores starting indices rather than copied suffixes. In a doubling round, rank[start] and rank[start + gap] describe the first and second halves; an out-of-range second half is treated as rank -1.

2. countSort shifts real ranks up by one so the missing-half marker uses key 0. It counts keys, converts counts into starting output positions, and places indices in their existing order. This stability lets the second-half sort followed by the first-half sort produce lexicographic rank-pair order.

3. Scanning sorted rank pairs assigns the next ranks. Equal pairs keep the same rank and different pairs get a new one. Doubling gap increases the compared prefix length each round. If all n ranks are distinct, the current suffix order is already final, so the loop can stop.

4. The inverse array pos locates each suffix in sorted order. Kasai’s scan compares it with its predecessor. After moving the original start forward by one, at least common - 1 leading matches remain reusable when common was positive; the code subtracts one and compares only beyond that known prefix. The first sorted suffix has no predecessor and receives LCP zero.

5. lcp[i] measures the match with the previous suffix and lcp[i + 1] the match with the next. Suffixes sharing a prefix occupy a contiguous sorted group, so the larger neighboring LCP is also the longest match against any other suffix. One more element is therefore unique if it exists. Minimize these fitting lengths to obtain the answer.

solutions.title: Suffix automaton
solutions.approach: Build a suffix automaton that groups subarrays sharing the same ending positions. Add each node’s occurrence count to its shorterId parent after processing its children. For a node seen exactly once, nodes[shorterId].maxLength + 1 is its shortest unique length; take the minimum of those lengths.
notes: Preserved naming: currNum, newId, lastId, shorterId, nextId, cloneId, ROOT_ID, and NO_ID. Transitions remain plain JavaScript objects.
solutions.intuition: Different subarrays can occur at exactly the same ending positions. A suffix automaton groups them into states, and every subarray represented by one state has the same occurrence count. Once a state’s count is known to be one, its shortest represented length is a unique-subarray candidate. This lets us examine groups of subarrays instead of checking each one separately.
hints: Group subarrays by their set of ending positions. All lengths represented by the same state then share one occurrence count.
Give each state created for an input position an initial count of 1, but give a clone count 0. Add child counts into shorterId parents only after processing the children.
A non-root state represents lengths from its shorterId parent’s maxLength + 1 through its own maxLength. If its final count is 1, consider the smallest length in that interval.

pseudocode.concept: Count occurrences of suffix-automaton states and take the shortest length represented by a state seen once.
steps: Start with the root state and extend the automaton once for each input value.
Create a new state with initial occurrence count 1, then add missing transitions while following shorterId links.

When an existing transition has the required length, link to it. Otherwise clone its transitions with the shorter required length and count 0, redirect the affected transitions, and link both states to the clone.
Turn shorterId links into a parent-to-children tree and record a traversal that visits parents before children.
Read that traversal backward, adding each non-root state’s count to its shorterId parent.
For every non-root state with count 1, consider its parent’s maximum length plus one.
Return the smallest candidate length.

solutions.explanation:
1. A state groups subarrays with the same set of ending positions. Its maxLength is the longest represented length; its shorterId parent describes a shorter suffix class. All represented lengths lie from the parent’s maxLength + 1 through the state’s maxLength, and all have the same occurrence count.

2. Each appended input value creates one new state with count 1 because it contributes one new ending position. The loop follows shorterId links to add missing transitions. If it reaches an existing transition whose target length is exactly one more than the source length, that target is the correct shorterId parent.

3. If the target length is too large, splitNode creates a clone for the shorter paths. It copies the target’s transitions, redirects the affected transitions to the clone, and makes the old target and the new state link to that clone. The clone starts with count 0 because splitting a class does not create another input position.

4. The shorterId links form a tree. Visiting parents first and then reversing the visit order ensures every child has accumulated its descendants’ counts before contributing to its parent. This produces the true number of ending positions for each state, including overlapping occurrences.

5. A state with final count 1 represents only unique subarrays. Its shortest represented length, nodes[shorterId].maxLength + 1, is therefore its best candidate. States with larger counts contribute none. Taking the minimum across all non-root states covers every possible subarray length and returns the shortest unique one.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: Count states and transitions over the entire construction, rather than multiplying the apparent nested loops.

phases.label: Extend the suffix automaton, create clones, and redirect transitions
Build the shorterId tree and record its traversal
Propagate occurrence counts once per non-root state
Inspect each state for its shortest unique length

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: A suffix automaton has O(n) states and transitions, and its extension and redirection work is amortized linear. Plain-object transition lookup is treated as expected constant time. Copying a clone’s transition object costs its number of entries, not O(1); summed across clones, those copied entries occupy distinct transitions in the final O(n)-transition automaton, so their total copy work is O(n). States, transitions, tree edges, and traversal arrays also use O(n) space.
